More research is required to definitively show that there is a link between CCT of the light source and discomfort glare. 2.2.3.2 Sky Glow There are generally two types of sky glow: natural and artificial. Natural sky glow is produced by the sun and moon when light is scattered within the atmosphere. The effect of this is small, roughly measured at 0.0002 cd/m2 (Boyce, 2009). Artificial sky glow occurs when light from buildings, roadways, stadiums and other man-made sources cause glare, or light scatter, upward into the sky. As Boyce (2009) states, artificial lighting is used by both private and public entities to provide safety, enhance the feeling of safety, and in the case of businesses, to improve attractiveness. The factors associated with sky glow extend beyond light itself. Variables such as the observer’s location, luminaire characteristics, the size of the city or town, the atmospheric conditions (aerosol content), spectral sensitivity of the detector being used to assess sky glow (Rea & Bierman, 2015), and the phase of the moon can all affect the amount of sky glow. It is widely known that shorter wavelength light has a greater impact on sky glow. Research comparing the sky glow of cities before and after retrofits that converted HPS systems to LED systems estimated sky glow to be nearly the same if not improved (Kinzey et al., 2017). Fortunately, adaptive lighting control systems have demonstrated they can effectively reduce the total amount of light scatter and, as a result, sky glow. Controlling the amount of flux, or energy of light emitted per second in lumens, is important for reducing sky glow; however, the most important aspect to minimizing light scatter is regulating the spectral content of the source. Moving to a lower CCT could further reduce the effect of sky glow, yet because of the spectral content of the light source, a lower CCT will not guarantee any reduction (Kinzey et al., 2017). Because LEDs have higher energies in the blue wavelengths, they tend to scatter more in the atmosphere (Garstang, 1986; Luginbuhl et al., 2012). Sky glow masks the ability to see stars in the night sky, which poses problems for astronomers. Sky glow is a result of improperly aimed or designed luminaires and light reflected from illuminated surfaces. Research recommends the use of monochromatic light sources like narrow spectrum amber LEDs or LPS lamps to reduce sky glow (Luginbuhl et al., 2012). The International Dark-Sky Association (2010) recommends the use of light sources with spectral power distributions that have wavelengths higher than 500 nm to reduce sky glow. 24 2.2.3.3 Ecology Both the presence and the spectral power distribution of the roadway lighting have raised concerns not in the areas of health and environment but also in ecology. 2.2.3.3.1 Wildlife Street lighting tends to have a negative effect on animals by disrupting their habitats or disorientating them or disturbing their circadian rhythms (van Bommel,
